topic: Kotlin types, null safety & smart casts

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `s?.length` evaluates to null because `s` is null, so the elvis operator supplies -1. `isNullOrEmpty()` is an extension on `String?`, so it can be called without `?.` and returns true for null. Nothing prints the literal `null` here.

questions.question: What is the inferred type of `x`?
questions.explanation: The compiler takes the common supertype of the branches: `Int` and `Nothing?` (the type of `null`). That common supertype is `Int?`. It does not widen to `Any?` because `Int?` already covers both branches.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: After `is Int` the parameter `x` is smart cast to `Int`, so `x + 1` is arithmetic (42), not string concatenation. `is String` smart casts to `String`, giving length 3. A `Double` matches neither branch, so it falls to `else`.

questions.question: This code does not compile. What is the reason, and what is the usual fix?
options: The null check must use `!==` instead of `!=` for the compiler to treat it as a type check
Smart casts never work on properties, only on local variables; the property must be made `lateinit`
`u.name` is a `var` that could change after the check; copy it to a local `val` or use `?.let`
`println` cannot take an `Int` from a nullable chain; the call must be written as `u.name!!.length`
questions.explanation: A `var` property can be changed by other code or another thread after the null check, so the compiler cannot prove it is still non-null. Copying it to a local `val` (or using `?.let`) gives a stable value that smart casts. Smart casts do work on stable `val` properties in the same module, so 'never on properties' is wrong.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `s` is not null, so the `let` block runs, but it returns null because the length is 6. The elvis operator looks at the result of the whole `s?.let { }` expression, not at `s`, so null from the lambda also triggers "fallback". This is a common bug when `?.let { } ?: ...` is used as an if/else.

questions.question: `lateinit var count: Int` is a valid declaration inside a class.
questions.explanation: `lateinit` is only allowed on non-null types that are not primitive types, because the 'not initialized' state is represented by a null reference in the field. For an `Int` you would use `Delegates.notNull()`, a nullable type, or a default value.

questions.question: Which statements about Kotlin's type hierarchy are true? Select all that apply.
options: A block-body function with no declared return type returns `Any`
`Nothing` is a subtype of every type, so a `throw` can be used where a `String` is expected
`Int` and `Int?` always compile to the same JVM type
`Unit` and `Nothing` are interchangeable as function return types
`Any?` is the top type; `Any` is not a supertype of `String?`
questions.explanation: `Nothing` has no values and is a subtype of every type, which is why `val n = x ?: throw ...` keeps the non-null type. `Any` only covers non-null types; `Any?` is the true top. `Unit` is a real value while `Nothing` means the function never returns; `Int?` is boxed to `java.lang.Integer` while `Int` is usually a primitive `int`; and a block-body function without a declared type returns `Unit`.

questions.question: A Java method `String getName()` has no nullability annotations and returns null. Which statement about the two Kotlin lines is correct?
questions.code:
val a: String = j.name   // line 1
val b = j.name           // line 2
println(b.length)
options: Neither line throws; both `a` and `b` hold null until a member is accessed
Line 1 fails to compile, because a platform type cannot be assigned to a non-null type
Line 1 throws at the assignment; line 2 holds null and fails later at `b.length`
Both lines throw at the assignment, because Kotlin null-checks every Java return value
questions.explanation: `j.name` has the platform type `String!`, so Kotlin lets you treat it as either nullable or non-null. When you assign it to a declared non-null `String`, the compiler inserts a null check that throws immediately. With an inferred type, `b` stays `String!` and holds null, so the failure moves to the later dereference, far from the real cause.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: The stdlib defines `operator fun String?.plus(other: Any?): String`, so `s + "!"` compiles without a safe call and turns the null receiver into the text "null". The result is the non-null string "null!" of length 5. It does not throw and does not drop the null.

questions.question: Which exceptions do `x!!`, `requireNotNull(x)` and `checkNotNull(x)` throw when `x` is null?
options: `!!` throws IllegalStateException, while `requireNotNull` and `checkNotNull` throw NullPointerException
All three throw NullPointerException; the helpers only differ by attaching a lazily built message
questions.explanation: `require*` functions express a bad argument (IllegalArgumentException) and `check*` functions express bad state (IllegalStateException), matching `require()` and `check()`. `!!` throws a NullPointerException. Choosing the right one makes crash reports say whether the caller or the object's state was wrong. The two helpers also smart cast `x` to non-null afterwards.
